prompt: A disease affects $2$ percent of a population. A screening test is positive for $90$ percent of people who have the disease and also positive for $5$ percent of people who do not. If a randomly chosen person tests positive, what is the probability they actually have the disease? Give a decimal to three places.
hint: The condition is a positive test, so the question is what fraction of all positive results come from people who really have the disease.

hints.text: The condition is a positive test, so the question is what fraction of all positive results come from people who really have the disease.

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Warm up: out of 100 people, if 10 are sick and all test positive, and 9 healthy people also test positive, then $P(\text{sick} \mid \text{positive}) = \frac{10}{19}$. Same counting with this problem's numbers.
True positives: $0.02 \times 0.90 = 0.018$. False positives: $0.98 \times 0.05 = 0.049$. All positives total $0.067$, so divide the true positives by that total.
$\frac{0.018}{0.067} \approx 0.269$, so only about $27$ percent of people who test positive have the disease.

explanation: A tree gives the two ways to test positive: disease ($0.02$) then positive ($0.90$) is $0.018$, and no disease ($0.98$) then positive ($0.05$) is $0.049$.
Adding the two routes gives the chance of any positive result: $P(\text{positive}) = 0.018 + 0.049 = 0.067$.
The conditional probability is the true-positive share of all positives: $\frac{0.018}{0.067} \approx 0.269$.
The answer is about $0.269$. Because the disease is rare, most positives are false positives from the large healthy group.

alternativeExplanations.title: Count 1,000 people
steps: 20 have the disease; 18 of them test positive. 980 do not; $0.05 \times 980 = 49$ of them test positive anyway.
Positives: $18 + 49 = 67$ people, of whom 18 are truly sick.

alternativeExplanations.title: The trap: answering 0.90
steps: $0.90$ is $P(\text{positive} \mid \text{disease})$: the chance a sick person tests positive.
The question flips the condition: $P(\text{disease} \mid \text{positive})$. These are different, and here very different.
Always write down which event is the condition before computing.
